41_marg2535: The word of the Lord. Jerome: Pethuel, the father of the prophet Joel, was called Bethuel by the Seventy translators. But since Bethuel means nothing at all in Hebrew, it is better to read Pethuel, which means “breadth” or “God opening.” Hence in Mark: “Ephpheta, that is, Be opened.” And well is Joel, who could say to the people: “Our mouth is open to you, O ye Corinthians, our heart is enlarged,” and who heard from the Lord: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it,” called the son of Pethuel, that is, of God, in whose power it is to open the mouth of man and to enlarge the holy man himself until he comes to perfection. Of this Pethuel, then, Joel is the son, that is, “beginning,” or “he is God”: for he who knows himself a beginner must grow through humility, so that with Moses he may hear: “He who is, hath sent me,” that is, the true God, as distinct from those who are not true gods. To this Joel, then, rightly came the word of the Lord, which was in the beginning with God. Further, it is said to come, not as regards itself, but as regards him to whom it comes; hence: “he is become my salvation.” So the word came, that is, the word spoke to the prophet.

41_marg2537: The palmer-worm is a worm found mostly among vegetables. The young of the locust before it has wings is called the bruchus; then, when it begins to fly a little, it is called the locust or attelabus; and when it flies fully, it is called the locust. The bruchus is much more harmful than the locust or the attelabus, for, lying in one place, it eats up the fruits to the root. Mildew is when the tender crops are struck by a harmful dew, and both stalk and ears turn the red of vermilion or of ochre. If these come one by one they are harmful; but if they all come together, they carry off everything entirely. And it could have happened historically that all these came together in the times of King Ahab and Elijah, when there was so great a famine for three years and six months that mothers are recorded to have eaten their sons.

41_marg2540: Allegorically: By the palmer-worm are signified the Assyrians or Chaldeans, who took captive the ten tribes in the time of Hezekiah, and the two, with the priestly tribe, in the time of Jehoiachin, the grandson of Josiah. By the locust, the Medes and Persians, who, when the empire of the Chaldeans was overthrown, held the Jews captive, though many of the two tribes returned with Zerubbabel by Cyrus’s leave. By the bruchus, the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander, above all Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who settled in Judea like the bruchus and devoured all that the former kings had left; under him were the wars of the Maccabees. By the mildew, the Romans, who utterly laid waste all Judea, overthrew its cities, burnt the temple of the Lord, and carried off the whole people by famine, sword and captivity.
41_marg2541: In the moral sense: By these four are signified four passions of the mind, which, if they rule beyond measure, take away the soul’s salvation. Two are of the present: sorrow at present adversity, and joy at present prosperity. Two are of the future: fear of evil to come, and hope of good to come. But the strong man ought so to bear himself that he neither rushes into any evil through present or hoped-for prosperity, nor is troubled beyond measure by present or future adversity. Otherwise: I think the palmer-worm is the passion as it begins in the mind, which is slow and cannot run about, and by stubborn lingering drinks up all the greenness. If we do not kill it in ourselves, it grows and flies, and now devours whatever it touches, now leaves things half-eaten and goes on to others; and, returning to its former seat, it becomes the bruchus, so that by its slowness it devours not only the leaves and bark but the pith. And if, as rarely happens, some breath of life remains after the bruchus, the mildew lays everything waste, turning even the stubble and the worthless hay black, so that they are useful neither for food nor even for dung.

41_marg2548: By the metaphor of the locusts he signifies the coming of the enemy, namely, of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Medes and Persians, and at last the Romans. And it is to be noted that the fierceness of the enemy is so told under the figure of the locusts that he compares the locusts themselves to the enemy; so that when you read of locusts you think of the enemy, and when you have thought of the enemy, you come back to the locusts.
41_marg2549: Allegorically: The nation of the princes of this world and of darkness comes up upon the land of God, that is, the human soul; for every soul of man is the land of God. Hence: “As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine.” The teeth of this nation are like the teeth of a lion, for “your adversary, the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about, seeking whom he may devour.” The lion’s whelp is the Antichrist, or a perverse doctrine. If this nation comes up upon us, at once it lays waste the vineyard, that is, the heart, from which ought to come the wine that gladdens; and it peels off the bark of our fig trees, so that we have not the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, and so that the holy man may not rest under our fig tree or vine while he fears the onset of the adversaries. Nor is that enough for this nation, unless it searches out and kills whatever is alive, so that, all the greenness consumed, the little branches remain white and dead, and that is fulfilled in us: “If in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?”

41_marg2550: As a young bride who loses her bridegroom in the flower of his youth girds herself with sackcloth and weeps, so the prophet urges the Israelites likewise to weep for the loss of the almighty bridegroom, whom they lost from the time they worshipped idols in Egypt. This people was a virgin in the patriarchs and prophets, by virginity of mind, and by the knowledge and worship of the true God; but after the idols it became an adulteress. Yet even this harlot the bridegroom takes as his wife in Hosea, bringing her, that is, out of the filth of the Gentiles. This can be said of any soul: if it has believed God from its earliest age, it has God for its virgin bridegroom; if anyone returns to the light of faith from among the Jews or pagans or heretics, he has a bridegroom indeed, but not a virgin one.

41_marg2553: All these things can be seen to have happened among the Jewish people for the sin of Christ’s Passion, when Jerusalem was laid waste by the Romans with famine and sword, and all joy and all the observances of the law failed. Daily too, when the Church, founded by Christ’s teaching, is separated from the bridegroom by sin, there perishes in it the sacrifice of an afflicted spirit and the wine that “may cheer the heart of man”; and as iniquity abounds, the teachers of the Church grieve that the virtues fail and the vices increase: for there fails the wheat of faith, the wine of spiritual understanding, the oil of mercy, and the barley of simplicity, or of keeping the letter. 41_marg2569: It is to be noted that neither the prophet nor the people would cry to the Lord except through the taking away of their delights. This can be referred to a man once just, who, when he has turned aside from justice and done evil, his former virtues will not profit him, but God will judge him in what he finds him in. Mystically, the wilderness figures the Gentiles, bereft by idolatry of the flower of the virtues. Or according to the saying: “for many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that hath a husband,” the beautiful places of this wilderness, that is, good works and virtues, the fire, that is, the devil, devours, as flame consumes stubble. But against these arrows of the devil we must cry like a thirsting garden bed, that the dew of divine mercy may quench them. Otherwise, by the springs that are dried up can be understood the teaching of Christ, which is dried up in those who have withdrawn from God, by the fire of lust, vainglory, gluttony and anger.
